digest.intro: Geopolitics pivots, enzymes de-age tissue, and one underscore destroyed a life.

items.title: Iran-US ceasefire holding; Qatar and Pakistan carrying messages between Washington and Tehran
items.blurb: The ceasefire that's been threading through recent briefings has reached a pivot: mediators report genuine progress, a Saudi nuclear deal was announced alongside it, and the Strait of Hormuz negotiations remain the fragile hinge. Qatar and Pakistan as simultaneous back-channels is the unusual diplomatic architecture worth watching.

items.title: Zelenskyy meets new UK PM Burnham on aircraft carrier — UK transfers drone jamming system designs to Ukraine
items.blurb: Andy Burnham's first foreign meeting as Prime Minister was with Zelenskyy aboard an aircraft carrier — already a statement — but the substantive news is the transfer of actual drone jamming system schematics, not hardware. Handing over design files rather than finished weapons is a quiet escalation in how deeply the UK is now embedding itself in Ukraine's defense architecture.

items.title: 7.1 earthquake in Japan
items.blurb: A significant 7.1 struck today — the JMA primary data is the cleanest place to track it, bypassing the noise of breaking-news amplification. Worth a check if you have any presence or connections in Japan.

items.title: One missing underscore sent an innocent man to prison for 18 months
items.blurb: Police were hunting a Kik user named "fus__ro_dah" (two underscores) and accidentally pulled records for "fus_ro_dah" (one underscore) — a different person entirely. Brandon Klayme was arrested in 2020, convicted in 2023, sentenced in 2024, served the full 18 months, and only had his conviction overturned this week when the typo surfaced during appeal prep. No evidence of the crime was ever found on his devices; the system just kept moving.

items.title: Anthropic's formal position on open-weights models
items.blurb: Dario Amodei uses this post to explicitly reject calls for banning Chinese open-weights models while making a more precise argument: his two actual nightmare scenarios are authoritarian-built models achieving military superiority, and AI-enabled deep repression — neither of which a ban on model weights addresses. The document is most useful as a forcing function for reading his earlier "Adolescence of Technology" essay, which laid these positions out six months ago and is still the cleaner piece.

items.title: $500 RL fine-tune of a 9B model beating frontier models on a narrow task
items.blurb: The playbook is now legible: take an open-weights model, label your proprietary workflow, run reinforcement learning against a scored version of the task. Bridgewater got 30% fewer errors than GPT-4-class on document relevance filtering; Harvey got a legal agent that outperforms GPT-5.5 on due diligence rubrics. The architecture insight is that frontier generality is actively a liability for tasks where "good" means "matches our internal judgment" — and RL on domain labels is the cheapest path to encoding that judgment.

items.title: Enzyme engineered to clear AGEs from the extracellular matrix — early longevity mechanism, not a supplement
items.blurb: Advanced glycation end-products accumulate in connective tissue over time, jamming collagen crosslinking and triggering chronic inflammation — they're implicated in diabetes, kidney disease, and general tissue aging. Researchers at Revel Pharmaceuticals used genetic selection in modified E. coli to evolve CMLase, an enzyme that breaks down a specific AGE called N(6)-Carboxymethyllysine. Testing is currently in model proteins, not humans — early-stage, but the mechanism is real and the approach (engineering enzymes via directed evolution) is serious.

items.title: Ars Astronomica — first English translations of medieval Hebrew and Latin astronomy manuscripts
items.blurb: A small scholarly imprint is doing the work: translating texts that span centuries of cosmological argument — including Gersonides' 136-chapter mathematical astronomy, which was never printed and survives only in manuscript — so that Hebrew and Latin sources can finally be read side by side in one language. The detail that stops you: the 1613 author David Gans wrote his Hebrew astronomy textbook having personally visited Tycho Brahe in Denmark. Someone is doing this obsessively, outside any institution, because no one else will.

facts.fact: Brandon Klayme's wrongful conviction for child sex abuse charges was triggered by a single missing underscore character in a Kik username — no evidence of the crime was ever found on his devices, yet he served the full 18-month sentence before the typo was discovered during appeal prep.

Revel Pharmaceuticals used directed evolution in genetically modified E. coli to engineer CMLase, an enzyme that breaks down a specific advanced glycation end-product (AGE) that accumulates in the extracellular matrix and inhibits collagen crosslinking — no such enzyme existed before this work.

A Harvey legal AI agent built via reinforcement learning on an open-weight model now outperforms both GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8 on the firm's own due-diligence rubrics — at a fraction of frontier inference costs.

Gersonides' 136-chapter mathematical astronomy — one of the medieval period's most significant astronomical works — was never printed and survives only in manuscript; Ars Astronomica is producing its first-ever English translation.

The 1613 Hebrew astronomer David Gans personally visited Tycho Brahe in Denmark and then wrote a Hebrew textbook weaving cutting-edge European astronomy together with medieval Jewish cosmological tradition — a direct link between the Tychonic and Jewish intellectual worlds.

make_something.prompt: Take a piece of text you wrote — an email, a note, anything — and render it as a 3D object whose geometry encodes meaning: word length as height, sentence structure as branching, punctuation as vertices. The AGE enzyme story and the underscore prison story both hinge on the idea that small syntax errors in data structures carry catastrophic weight. What does your own writing look like when its structure is the surface?

art_picks.title: Leviathan
art_picks.creator: Lucien Castaing-Taylor & Véréna Paravel
art_picks.why: A sensory assault shot almost entirely with GoPros lashed to fishing nets, hooks, and the bodies of workers — it dissolves the line between documentary and pure texture, turning industrial labor at sea into something hallucinatory and abstract. No narration, no explanation; just the system laid bare as an overwhelming physical experience.

art_picks.title: Paul Thek: Dream of Vanishing
art_picks.creator: Paul Thek
art_picks.why: Pace Gallery's current show surfaces Thek's rarely seen late works — newspaper paintings, canvas pieces, quilted flags — from an artist who spent his career building elaborate ritual environments that collapsed the sacred and the abject, the handmade and the mythological. The kind of obsessive, category-destroying practice that makes you want to throw out your rules.

art_picks.title: Rejoicing in the Hands
art_picks.creator: Devendra Banhart
art_picks.why: A deeply personal 2004 record where folk, nonsense language, and hand-drawn cosmology fuse into something that feels like a private ritual made public — each song a small handmade system with its own internal logic. Expressive surface, weird structure underneath; the kind of thing that sounds like someone went unreasonably deep on a narrow obsession.

events.name: Whitney Biennial 2026
events.venue: Whitney Museum of American Art, 99 Gansevoort St, Manhattan
events.why: The 82nd edition threads together infrastructure, interspecies kinship, and what 'American' even means now — with standout works like AI sculptures synthesizing dead artists' social-media trails and a large-scale piece made from US military night-vision goggles; it's a biennial with actual conceptual teeth, closing soon.

events.name: Gabriel Orozco: Public Nature
events.venue: JCDecaux Bus Shelters across New York City
events.why: Orozco's first major NYC public commission places 10 new site-specific photographs — capturing found objects and ephemeral urban interventions — inside bus shelters citywide, turning the city's own infrastructure into a gallery and the daily commute into an act of noticing.

events.name: UBB 40th Anniversary: BreakBeat Lou, Lord Finesse, Diamond D, Grand Puba & more
events.why: A free celebration of Ultimate Breaks and Beats — the 1986 series that quietly became the most-sampled record collection in hip-hop history — with the original architects performing live; a rare chance to see the invisible infrastructure of modern music made audible and present.

events.name: MoMA PS1 Warm Up 2026
events.venue: MoMA PS1 Courtyard, 22-25 Jackson Ave, Long Island City, Queens
events.why: The 28th season of PS1's outdoor electronic series runs Fridays through August, with a 2026 lineup pulling from dub, gabber, house, hyperpop, and avant-garde improvisation — the July 31 edition falls squarely in the window, and the museum galleries (including Precious Okoyomon's living forest installation) stay open late.

events.name: Andrew Bird with the Wordless Music Orchestra: 20th Anniversary of 'The Mysterious Production of Eggs'
events.why: Bird performs his 2005 baroque-folk-loop record in full for the first time ever, backed by a full orchestra — a singular, unrepeatable event for an album built on elaborate multi-tracked violin loops and handcrafted avant-pop systems; free admission.
